# CHAPTER XX

## FAILURE (1871)

Far back in childhood, Henry Adams could recall his first visit to Harvard College—nine years old, taken by his mother to his aunt at the old President's House. The house had an air of colonial self-respect that impressed even a child. When Adams closed his interview with President Eliot, he asked the Bursar about that drawing-room, for the house had been turned to base uses; the deserted kitchen adjacent was also to let. He took both. The standard was below that of Washington, but it was, for the moment, the best.

For the next nine months the Assistant Professor had no time to waste on comforts or amusements. He exhausted all his strength in trying to keep one day ahead of his duties. He could not stop to think whether he were doing the work rightly. He could not get it done to please him, rightly or wrongly, for he never could satisfy himself what to do.

The fault Adams had found with Harvard as an undergraduate must have been more or less just; the college had elected President Eliot in 1869 to carry out its reforms. The two Professors of History could not cover the ground. Between Gurney's classical courses and Torrey's modern ones lay a gap of a thousand years which Adams was to fill. Down to the moment he took his chair, he had given, as far as he could remember, an hour, more or less, to the Middle Ages.

Not that his ignorance troubled him! He knew enough to be ignorant. A parent gives life, but as parent, gives no more. A murderer takes life, but his deed stops there. A teacher affects eternity; he can never tell where his influence stops. A teacher must either treat history as a catalogue, a record, a romance, or as an evolution; and whether he affirms or denies evolution, he falls into all the burning faggots of the pit. He makes of his scholars either priests or atheists, plutocrats or socialists, judges or anarchists, almost in spite of himself. In essence incoherent and immoral, history had either to be taught as such—or falsified.

Adams wanted to do neither. He had no theory of evolution to teach, and could not make the facts fit one. He saw no relation between his students and the Middle Ages except the Church, where the ground was dangerous. The man who should bring the Middle Ages into the line of evolution would be a greater man than Lamarck or Linnæus; but history had nowhere broken down so pitiably. Since Gibbon, the spectacle was almost a scandal—a hundred years behind the experimental sciences, less instructive for serious purpose than Walter Scott and Alexandre Dumas.

The college expected him to teach the boys elementary dates and relations, that they might not be a disgrace to the university. He could frankly tell them that, provided they passed their examinations, they might get their facts where they liked, and use the teacher only for questions. The only privilege a student had that was worth claiming was that of talking to the professor. Any large body of students stifles the student. No man can instruct more than half-a-dozen at once.

The lecture system to classes of hundreds—very much that of the twelfth century—suited Adams not at all. The number of students whose minds were of an order above the average was barely one in ten; nine minds in ten take polish passively, like a hard surface; only the tenth sensibly reacts.

Adams thought he would try to cultivate this tenth mind, at the expense of the other nine. He acted on the rule that a teacher who knew nothing of his subject should not pretend to teach what he did not know, but should join his scholars in trying to find the best way of learning it. The pretentious name of historical method was sometimes given to this process, but the name smacked of German pedagogy, and a young professor who respected neither history nor method fell into trouble enough without adding a German parentage.

The task was doomed. Nothing is easier than to teach historical method, but, when learned, it has little use. History is a tangled skein one may take up at any point, and break when one has unravelled enough; but complexity precedes evolution. The Pteraspis grins horribly from the closed entrance. Adams took law as subject, the Law School as end, with half-a-dozen intelligent young men as victims. The course began in primitive man, and came down through the Salic Franks to the Norman English. The boys worked like rabbits, and learned to chase an idea, like a hare, through as dense a thicket of obscure facts as they were likely to meet at the bar; but their teacher knew the method led nowhere. Their science had no system, since its subject was merely antiquarian.

What was the use of training an active mind to waste its energy? The fault lay in the system, which could lead only to inertia. His mind required conflict, competition, contradiction even more than the student's. He would have seated a rival assistant professor opposite him, whose business should be strictly limited to expressing opposite views; but of all university freaks, no irregularity shocked the intellectual atmosphere so much as contradiction or competition between teachers. In that respect the thirteenth-century university system was worth the whole teaching of the modern school.

In spite of President Eliot's reforms and generous support, the system remained costly, clumsy and futile. Adams used his lost two years of German schooling to inflict their results on his students, and by happy chance was in the full tide of fashion. The Germans were crowning their new emperor at Versailles, and surrounding his head with a halo of Pepins and Merwigs, Othos and Barbarossas. He imposed Germany on his scholars with a heavy hand. The seven years he passed in teaching seemed to him lost.

The uses of adversity are beyond measure strange. As a professor, he regarded himself as a failure. He had tried a great many experiments, and wholly succeeded in none. He had succumbed to the weight of the system. He quitted the university at last, in 1877, with a feeling that, but for the invariable courtesy and kindness shown by every one in it, he should be sore at his failure.

These were his own feelings, but they were not felt in the college. With the same perplexing impartiality that had disconcerted him as an undergraduate, the college insisted on expressing the opposite view. When President Eliot hinted that Adams's services merited recognition, Adams could have wept in hysterics, so grateful was he; but he could not allow the college to think he esteemed himself entitled to distinction. Yet nothing in the vanity of life struck him as more humiliating than that Harvard College, which he had persistently criticised, abused, abandoned, and neglected, should alone have offered him a dollar, an office, an encouragement, or a kindness. Harvard College might have its faults, but at least it redeemed America, since it was true to its own.

The only part of education that the professor thought a success was the students. He found them excellent company. Cast in the same mould, without violent emotions or sentiment, and, except for American habits, ignorant of all man had ever thought or hoped, their minds burst open like flowers at the sunlight of a suggestion. Their faith in education was so full of pathos that one dared not ask what they thought they could do with education when they got it. Adams put the question to one, and was surprised at the answer: "The degree of Harvard College is worth money to me in Chicago." So far as it went, the answer settled one's doubts.

He never knew whether his colleagues shared his doubts about their own utility. Unlike himself, they knew their business. He could not tell his scholars that history glowed with social virtue; the Professor of Chemistry cared not a chemical atom whether society was virtuous. He could not pretend mediæval society proved evolution; the Professor of Physics smiled at evolution. Adams was glad to dwell on the virtues of the Church and the triumphs of its art; the Professor of Political Economy had to treat them as waste of force. They knew what they had to teach; he did not. They might perhaps be frauds without knowing it; but he knew certainly nothing else of himself. He could teach his students nothing; he was only educating himself at their cost.
